title: The Evergreen Game
transcript: The year is [music] 1852, and Adolf Anderssen is playing with the white pieces. A player so legendary [music] that not only one, but two of his games made the history of chess. It is pretty obvious [music] that this knight is hanging, but so is this one since the rook is creating a pin. If [music] we take that knight, this knight is going to get captured with a checkmate threat. And if G3, queen takes F2 [music] protected by the bishop is going to lead to a checkmate. So, it seems like if anything, black is playing for an advantage, [music] but the genius Anderssen finds the move rook A2 D1, [music] which is just the tip of the iceberg of the beauty of this position. Black thinks, "Well, this is just a free knight, and I still have the same checkmate threat." And so, takes the knight. [music] And it seems like mate is unstoppable, but black follows up with rook takes E7 [music] check. If black tries to ignore the rook, now rook takes D7 leads to a checkmating attack. And the only way to stop it is [music] going to be to sacrifice the black queen. But now, white is simply winning. But there's no need for any of that. The [music] black knight captures the rook, and now the light square bishop is joining the attack on the white king. And black would be completely winning if it wasn't [music] for the incredible queen takes D7. A queen sacrifice that has to be accepted because if [music] the king moves, this is simply going to be checkmate. So, the king takes. Now, white is only left [music] with two bishops and one rook against the queen, three minor pieces, and both rooks of black. [music] And white needs to be very careful because the double check bishop [music] to B5 is actually a blunder because the king runs out into E6, and there's no follow-up [music] after rook check. The bishop covers the check, and black is completely winning. So, instead, the winning move is bishop to F5. >> [music] >> Now, this is again a double check, meaning that the only move is for the king to move. But after the king moves, Adolf Anderssen follows [music] up with Bishop to D7 check. If the king comes back, this is a simple [music] checkmate, and the same exact thing happens if the king comes this way. >> [music] >> Bishop takes E7. It's a beautiful checkmate.
